video_title: Lawfare Daily: The Court Against the Courts with Steve Vladeck and Kate Klonick
gist: Steve Vladeck walks Kate Klonick through his Harvard Law Review Foreword, arguing that since early 2025 the U.S. Supreme Court has actively weakened federal district courts — via unexplained emergency-docket stays, the CASA limit on universal injunctions, channeling Alien Enemies Act and federal-money cases away from injunctive relief, and public criticism of district judges — while doing essentially nothing to defend them against a coordinated White House/DOJ/congressional delegitimization campaign that has produced impeachment resolutions against 13 district judges (versus zero under Biden). He argues the resulting collapse of trust and the erosion of appellate standards of review is a systemic governance risk, and that the correct fix is court reform that empowers district courts as an institution while curbing single-judge forum shopping — a fight he expects to become live around and after the midterms.

insights.claim: Steve Vladeck's 2025 Harvard Law Review Foreword argues that the defining feature of the U.S. Supreme Court since early 2025 is not its big doctrinal rulings but its adversarial posture toward the federal district courts beneath it.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
insights.so_what: Frames judicial-branch risk as internal (top court undercutting trial courts) rather than purely executive-versus-judiciary, which changes what reform proposals and litigation strategy should target.
insights.quote: the story of the Supreme Court since early 2025 is in the main a story about the court against the courts

insights.claim: Vladeck holds that the Supreme Court is not a passive bystander to executive-branch attacks on district judges but bears affirmative responsibility for escalating them.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
insights.so_what: If the top court is an accelerant rather than a brake, the probability of continued non-compliance with lower-court orders rises, raising the tail risk around any litigation-dependent policy or contract.
insights.quote: It's why I think the justices bear some responsibility for pouring gasoline on those fires.

insights.claim: Vladeck's sharpest formulation is that the Supreme Court is not merely acting without constraint but is actively narrowing what district courts are legally able to do.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
insights.so_what: A useful test for reading each new emergency-docket order: does it decide the merits, or does it shrink the toolkit of the courts that actually find facts?
insights.quote: It is not just doing whatever it wants. It is making it harder for district courts to do what they must.

insights.claim: Vladeck deliberately wrote an institutionalist rather than doctrinal Foreword — skipping the unitary-executive and Voting Rights Act cases — because he judged the Supreme Court's institutional relationship with lower courts to be the under-covered story of the term.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
insights.so_what: Signals where elite legal commentary is heading: away from case-by-case doctrine toward structural capacity of the judiciary, which is where reform legislation will eventually be aimed.

insights.claim: The main critique Vladeck says he receives — that the paper assumes district courts were substantively right — misreads a piece that deliberately avoids litigating the merits of individual rulings and rests instead on volume, threat, and appeal statistics.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
insights.so_what: The empirical framing makes the argument harder to dismiss on partisan grounds, increasing its odds of being cited in future reform hearings.

insights.claim: Vladeck argues that cherry-picking one aggressive district judge to indict hundreds is analytically invalid because the judges ruling against the administration are geographically diverse and include many Republican appointees.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
insights.so_what: Undercuts the 'rogue liberal judge' narrative used to justify structural attacks; watch whether the appointing-president breakdown of adverse rulings keeps staying bipartisan.
insights.quote: don't let the sort of the outliers come to define the the rest of the field

themes.theme: District court overload: the docket data

insights.claim: The Southern District of Indiana went from zero immigration detention cases in 2023 and one in 2024 to 450 since January 1 of last year — a surge in a district that is not a traditional hotbed of federal litigation.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that immigration-enforcement litigation load is national, not confined to border or blue-state districts; multiplied across 93 districts it implies systemic capacity strain and slower adjudication of everything else.
insights.quote: which had zero immigration detention cases in 2023, it had one in 2024, and since January 1st of last year, it's had 450

insights.claim: Klonick notes that the case volumes now hitting federal district courts resemble state and local court numbers, which is anomalous because federal courts are not courts of general jurisdiction.
insights.speaker: Kate Klonick
insights.so_what: Federal trial-court throughput is a hidden bottleneck for any party whose position depends on timely federal adjudication, from contractors to detained individuals.
insights.quote: these are numbers that you see in state, local courts

insights.claim: The pace of major federal appellate decisions has changed from roughly one weekly check-in fifteen years ago to three hundred-page rulings landing in quick succession on a single Friday afternoon.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
insights.so_what: Information overload means market-relevant legal rulings are systematically under-priced simply because no one can process them in real time — an edge for anyone with dedicated legal monitoring.
insights.quote: now at like 4:30 on a Friday afternoon, you'll get three of them in quick succession, and they're each like a hundred pages long

insights.claim: While district court dockets are exploding, the Supreme Court's own docket is at its smallest since roughly the Civil War era, according to Vladeck.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
insights.so_what: The workload asymmetry is the mechanism behind the empathy gap Vladeck describes, and it is the strongest factual hook for arguments that the Court should take more merits cases rather than fewer.
insights.quote: their docket's smaller today than it has been at any point since the civil

insights.claim: A plurality — though not a majority — of nationwide challenges to Trump policies have been filed in the District of Columbia, which Vladeck attributes to the government being headquartered there rather than to forum shopping.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
insights.so_what: Concentration in DC makes the DC district and DC Circuit the highest-leverage venues to monitor for policy-blocking rulings.
insights.quote: It is I think not a majority Kate but a plurality of all of the sort of nationwide challenges to Trump policies have been brought in DC.

insights.claim: Major litigation against the administration has been dispersed well beyond DC and Boston — including Minnesota, Oregon, Seattle, Chicago, Georgia and Texas — which Vladeck says undercuts the claim that adverse rulings are the product of hand-picked sympathetic judges.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
insights.so_what: Geographic dispersion means legal risk to federal policy is not containable by targeting a handful of districts, and reform proposals aimed at 'forum shopping' will not resolve it.

themes.theme: Doctrinal tools that shrank district-court power

insights.claim: The Supreme Court's CASA decision last June, split 6-3 along Republican/Democratic appointment lines, held that federal district courts generally cannot issue universal injunctions protecting non-plaintiffs.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
insights.so_what: Removes the single most powerful mechanism for pausing a federal policy nationwide, meaning affected parties must now litigate individually or via class/APA routes — slower and costlier relief.

insights.claim: The Fifth Circuit is now attempting to permit universal relief in the opposite ideological direction despite CASA, according to Vladeck.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
insights.so_what: Asymmetric application of CASA would make the Fifth Circuit a uniquely potent venue for challenges to future Democratic administrations — a durable, direction-dependent litigation risk.
insights.quote: even though the fifth circuit is now trying to say it can do it in the other direction

insights.claim: By foreclosing nationwide Administrative Procedure Act review of Alien Enemies Act cases, the Supreme Court prevented a single ruling from resolving the statute's legality and forced district-by-district habeas litigation instead.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
insights.so_what: Procedural channeling, not merits rulings, is how the legality of contested executive powers is kept unresolved indefinitely — a pattern worth watching in other emergency-power fights.

insights.claim: Vladeck flags the Tucker Act as an underappreciated lever: routing disputes over federal contracts and federal money to the Court of Federal Claims strips claimants of injunctive relief, leaving only a possible damages recovery years later.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
insights.so_what: Directly material for contractors, grantees and universities: a funding cutoff of $5 million or $500 million may be practically unstoppable in real time, so counterparty risk on federal money should be priced as if injunctive relief is unavailable.
insights.quote: if you're suing over, you know, $5 million or $500 million of federal funding being cut off and the best you can hope for is three years from now maybe you get some of the money back

insights.claim: The Supreme Court has repeatedly stayed district court rulings with no explanation, forcing lower courts to guess at what the Court wants and then criticizing them when they guess wrong.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
insights.so_what: Unexplained stays convert legal outcomes into low-visibility, hard-to-forecast events — raising the variance of any position dependent on a district-court injunction holding.

insights.claim: Justice Gorsuch's concurrence in the NIH case last August accused three different district courts of defying the Supreme Court for failing to follow unexplained or thinly explained orders issued in other cases.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
insights.so_what: A sitting justice publicly accusing trial courts of defiance supplies rhetorical ammunition to the political campaign against those same judges — an institutional feedback loop.

insights.claim: Vladeck argues the Supreme Court applies restrictions on nationwide relief to district courts while exempting itself from the same constraints.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
insights.so_what: The asymmetry is the core legitimacy vulnerability critics will press in any reform debate.

insights.claim: Justice Kavanaugh's CASA concurrence makes a two-step argument — that major new federal policies should get nationally uniform interim answers, and that the Supreme Court rather than district courts should supply them.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
insights.so_what: If adopted, this would make the emergency docket the de facto first-instance forum for national policy fights, compressing the timeline on which policy legality gets resolved.
insights.quote: we should provide interim answers that are nationally uniform

insights.claim: Vladeck calls Kavanaugh's position a perfect foil because the same CASA decision that claims only the Supreme Court can provide nationally uniform interim answers failed to provide one itself, merely erasing three district court rulings.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
insights.so_what: The gap between the announced role and actual output means litigants face a vacuum: neither district courts nor the Supreme Court currently supply timely nationwide answers.
insights.quote: Kavanagh says only we can play this role and oh by the way, we're not going to do it here

insights.claim: Vladeck describes the 'nine justice district court' concept as institutionally fascinating but legally unworkable because it ignores the statutory constraints that limit the Supreme Court's role in these cases.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
insights.so_what: Any reform premised on the Supreme Court absorbing trial-court functions would require statutory change, making it a congressional question rather than a judicial one.
insights.quote: it's a little bit lawless in that it doesn't account for all of the statutory constraints on the Supreme Court

insights.claim: Klonick argues that eight of the nine justices almost certainly do not want a nine-justice district court because the Court lacks the capacity and inclination to do fact-finding work.
insights.speaker: Kate Klonick
insights.so_what: Suggests the Kavanaugh model will not be institutionalized, leaving the current gap — restricted district courts plus an unwilling Supreme Court — as the persistent equilibrium.

insights.claim: In the Texas redistricting case, the Supreme Court stayed a 180-page opinion by a Trump-appointed district judge — issued by a three-judge court after major evidentiary hearings — in a five-paragraph order that never called the fact-finding clearly erroneous or even wrong.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
insights.so_what: Signals that trial-court fact-finding no longer reliably constrains outcomes, so evidentiary wins at the district level should be discounted when handicapping final results in high-salience cases.
insights.quote: the Supreme Court just staves that decision in a five paragraph order that never says the district court's factf finding was wrong um or even worse was clearly erroneous which is the standard they're supposed to follow

insights.claim: Klonick argues that standards of review — the rules restricting appellate courts to legal error rather than re-litigating facts — have effectively disintegrated and now go unmentioned in decisions.
insights.speaker: Kate Klonick
insights.so_what: Erosion of standards of review makes appellate outcomes far less predictable from trial records, raising litigation risk premiums across the board.

themes.theme: Defiance of orders and the collapse of government-court trust

insights.claim: In the Alien Enemies Act case, the government argued it was not bound by Judge Boasberg's on-the-record oral instruction to turn removal planes around because he had not separately memorialized it in a written order.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
insights.so_what: A government theory that oral judicial orders are non-binding, if left uncorrected, materially weakens emergency relief as a real-world constraint on executive action.
insights.quote: because he didn't separately memorialize that in a written order, um, it wasn't actually an or order that they, you know, were bound to follow

insights.claim: Boasberg only got the chance to rule at all because the ACLU learned at roughly 11 p.m. on a Friday that removals were imminent, which Vladeck cites as evidence the operation was designed to evade judicial review.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
insights.so_what: Where executive action is timed to outrun judicial process, the practical constraint becomes NGO monitoring speed rather than legal doctrine.

insights.claim: Despite the initial two flights proceeding, nobody has been removed from the country under the Alien Enemies Act since Boasberg's TROs, according to Vladeck.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
insights.so_what: Evidence that district court intervention, even when initially defied, produced durable practical constraint — the empirical core of the case against weakening trial courts.
insights.quote: nobody has been removed from the country under the Alien Enemies act since

insights.claim: The Supreme Court's 5-4 ruling in the Boasberg Alien Enemies case granted the government emergency relief on dubious technical venue grounds despite unclean hands, with Justice Sotomayor warning in dissent that this tells the government it faces no consequences and can repeat the conduct.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
insights.so_what: Establishes an incentive structure in which defying a district court order carries no cost, which should raise expected non-compliance in future emergency litigation.

insights.claim: The entire federal district court for the District of Maryland issued a standing order automatically staying removal for roughly 72 hours whenever a detained noncitizen files a habeas petition — and the Justice Department responded by suing the district court in a case called United States v. Russell.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
insights.so_what: The executive suing a court over its own protective order is a qualitatively new escalation and a leading indicator of open executive-judicial conflict.
insights.quote: the Justice Department sued the district court. Um, like there's a lawsuit out there right now called the United States versus Russell.

insights.claim: Klonick argues the plane-removal episode was a precedential wake-up call that destroyed trust between the government and courts nationwide, prompting judges like Judge Sooknanan to announce round-the-clock emergency availability.
insights.speaker: Kate Klonick
insights.so_what: Loss of the good-faith presumption changes judicial behavior structurally — faster TROs, standing orders, and less deference to government representations in all litigation, not just immigration.
insights.quote: It lost trust between the government and the and the courts all over the country.

insights.claim: Vladeck argues that most of the administration's conduct has not survived contact with federal judges, and that prosecutions collapse once subjected to judicial scrutiny because courts force sworn statements and expose filings to professional-misconduct risk.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
insights.so_what: Judicial process, not political opposition, is currently the binding constraint on executive action — so any structural weakening of courts translates directly into fewer checks.
insights.quote: so much of this administration's behavior has not survived contact with federal judges

themes.theme: The delegitimization campaign against district judges

insights.claim: Impeachment resolutions have now been introduced in the House against 13 different federal district judges, compared with zero during the entire Biden administration.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
insights.so_what: The cleanest quantitative marker of regime change in judicial-political norms; the count is a trackable indicator of escalation.
insights.quote: we are now up to 13 different federal district judges against whom impeachment resolutions have been introduced in the House of Representatives

insights.claim: Vladeck says there is sustained coordination among the White House, the Justice Department, and congressional Republicans behind the attacks on district judges, citing Ted Cruz's January Senate subcommittee hearing on impeaching Judges Boasberg and Boardman.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
insights.so_what: Coordinated rather than spontaneous attacks imply the campaign persists regardless of any single case outcome, and will scale with each adverse ruling.

insights.claim: Vladeck's central diagnosis is that the goal is not to remove individual judges but to delegitimize federal district courts as an institution.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
insights.so_what: Reframes the risk: even if no judge is ever removed, the campaign succeeds if compliance with district-court orders becomes optional.
insights.quote: The push is to delegitimize federal district courts

insights.claim: Vladeck distinguishes criticizing individual judges — which he did of Judge Kacsmaryk — from personal attacks and impeachment campaigns aimed at the judiciary's integrity, and says that line has been crossed repeatedly.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
insights.so_what: Provides the operative test for distinguishing normal criticism from institutional attack — useful for anyone assessing rule-of-law degradation.
insights.quote: you can criticize individual judges what you should not be doing is undermining the integrity of the federal judiciary

insights.claim: Vladeck attributes much of the anti-court campaign to Steven Miller and the White House rather than to a Federalist Society agenda, and says institutions that would historically have ignored Miller are now deferring to him because of his influence with the president.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
insights.so_what: Locates the driver in a single personnel node, meaning the intensity of the campaign is tied to that person's standing rather than to durable conservative legal doctrine.
insights.quote: I think a lot of this is coming from Steven Miller.

insights.claim: Vladeck identifies a genuine schism on the legal right between those who see the current moment as an unprecedented threat to the rule of law and those who do not see it or will not say so — a split visible both on the bench among Republican appointees and within the Federalist Society and conservative academia.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
insights.so_what: The 'principles versus Trump' split is the key variable determining whether adverse rulings keep coming from Republican-appointed judges — the single best predictor of continued judicial constraint.
insights.quote: principles versus Trump

insights.claim: Chief Justice Roberts has made only two public statements in 18 months about attacks on judges: a March statement that judges are appealed rather than impeached, and an unpublicized Rice University remark that 'these attacks have to stop' without identifying which attacks.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
insights.so_what: Quantifies the Court's institutional silence; any escalation in Roberts's public defense of lower courts would be a meaningful signal of shifting judicial posture.
insights.quote: We don't impeach judges when we disagree with them. We appeal their rulings.

themes.theme: Judicial rhetoric as an outlet of last resort

insights.claim: Vladeck argues the rise of rhetorical, attention-seeking district court opinions reflects judges having no outlet other than their decisions to signal government conduct they consider unprecedented — they cannot hold press conferences or go on television.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
insights.so_what: Opinion rhetoric becomes a readable stress indicator: escalating tone in trial-court opinions signals escalating perceived executive lawlessness.

insights.claim: Vladeck draws a sharp line between rhetorical opinions that undermine their own credibility and those that use only the government's own material, contrasting a five-page Bible-passage-laden habeas grant with an 83-page ruling whose only images were screenshots of the government's own tweets.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
insights.so_what: A practical rubric for judging whether an unusual opinion will survive appellate review or become a liability for the position it defends.
insights.quote: the only picture she used were screenshots of the government's own tweets

insights.claim: The Codes of Conduct Committee of the Judicial Conference of the United States issued a new advisory opinion earlier this year encouraging judges to speak publicly about threats to the rule of law.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
entities: Judicial Conference of the United States
insights.so_what: An obscure but concrete institutional shift: expect more extrajudicial judicial commentary, which will itself become a flashpoint in the executive-judiciary conflict.

insights.claim: Klonick warns that celebrating rhetorically aggressive district court opinions is self-defeating even when one agrees with the outcome, because the breakdown of judicial form is itself the symptom of systemic failure.
insights.speaker: Kate Klonick
insights.so_what: Suggests reputational and doctrinal costs accumulate on both sides, accelerating erosion of the norms that make court orders self-enforcing.

insights.claim: Vladeck's reform menu includes three-judge district courts, random nationwide case assignment, a Washington venue default, Judicial Conference guidance, relaxed qualified immunity, and codifying Bivens damages actions.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
insights.so_what: This is the concrete legislative agenda that would surface if court reform becomes live; each item has distinct winners and losers among litigants against the federal government.

insights.claim: Vladeck's organizing principle is to empower district courts in the plural while making it harder for litigants to hand-pick a single judge capable of shutting down nationwide policy.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
insights.so_what: This is the likeliest bipartisan landing zone for reform because it cuts against single-judge power that both parties have exploited.
insights.quote: we should be empowering the district courts plural, right? While making it harder for litigants to abuse which district judges they actually appear before

insights.claim: Vladeck argues court reform should be reframed as accountability reform — fixing the relationship between the judiciary and the other branches — rather than as Supreme Court reform.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
insights.so_what: Shifts the reform target from court-packing and term limits toward remedies, venue, and damages actions — a less headline-grabbing but more legislatively tractable agenda.
insights.quote: I want court reform to not just be about Supreme Court reform. I want court reform to be about accountability reform.

insights.claim: Vladeck rejects Garrett West's Virginia Law Review argument that the emergency docket's rise stems from suing the government being too easy, holding the opposite view that it is far too hard to sue the federal government — noting one cannot sue federal officers for damages for constitutional violations, a point on which he lost 5-4 at the Supreme Court.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
insights.so_what: Frames the intellectual fault line in the reform debate; whichever diagnosis wins determines whether remedies expand or contract for parties harmed by federal action.
insights.quote: it is way too hard to sue the federal government

insights.claim: Vladeck says court reform is now genuinely 'in the water' in a way it has not been in his professional career, and dismisses Biden's Presidential Commission on Supreme Court Reform as designed never to accomplish anything beyond sparing Biden from taking a position during the 2020 election.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
entities: Presidential Commission on Supreme Court Reform
insights.so_what: Signals a real policy window opening rather than symbolic study commissions — relevant for anyone modeling legal-regime change over the next election cycle.
insights.quote: I do think court reform is now in the water um in a way that it has not been in my professional career

insights.claim: Vladeck expects the substantive court reform conversation to be roughly two and a half years away, while Klonick expects the debate to begin shortly after the midterms.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
insights.so_what: A dated timeline for when judiciary-structure legislation becomes a live political risk, useful for positioning around policy-sensitive litigation exposure.
insights.quote: a much broader court reform conversation that I hope right we're you know two and a half years away from having

insights.claim: Vladeck says he wants to die on the hill of opposing the emerging progressive-academic movement — associated with forthcoming books from Nicholas Bagley and from Niko Bowie and a co-author — that argues the way out of the crisis is to weaken the courts.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
insights.so_what: An intra-left fight over judicial power is forming; its outcome shapes whether a future Democratic Congress strengthens or dismantles judicial checks.
insights.quote: there's a move of foot especially among progressive academics to suggest that the way out of this is to weaken the courts

insights.claim: Vladeck's empirical case against weakening the judiciary rests on outcomes that would not have occurred without powerful district judges, including the Abrego Garcia case and Judge John Bates blocking the executive order targeting law firms.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
insights.so_what: Concrete precedent that district courts are the operative protection for targeted private firms — relevant to any business assessing exposure to retaliatory executive action.
insights.quote: we are not set up in our current political system to live in a world in which the federal judiciary in general has no power to stand up to the executive branch

insights.claim: Vladeck argues the Chief Justice's constitutional title — Chief Justice of the United States, not of the Supreme Court — carries an unfulfilled duty to supervise and defend the entire federal judiciary.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
insights.so_what: Provides the rhetorical framing reform advocates will use to pressure Roberts personally; his response is the single highest-leverage variable inside the judiciary.
insights.quote: Mr. Chief Justice, you are not the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court. You are the Chief Justice of the United States.

insights.claim: Vladeck contends the justices are structurally insulated — attending circuit judicial conferences only to deliver canned remarks — and that this bubble causes them to affect district courts in ways they do not intend or fully perceive.
insights.speaker: Steve Vladeck
insights.so_what: If the problem is information rather than intent, targeted evidence campaigns like the Foreword could plausibly change behavior — a rare optimistic channel in an otherwise deteriorating picture.
insights.quote: I think the court is just too damn cloistered.
